p-kadikoy.angle_note: one home for the Kadıköy market and the Tuesday pazar

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Güneşlibahçe Sokağı
old_cards.teaser: Five minutes uphill from the ferry: the fish row, the butchers and the greengrocers that feed Kadıköy's own kitchens.
old_cards.body: The market is not a building, it is a grid of short streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, and Güneşlibahçe Sokağı is its spine — OpenStreetMap maps fishmongers at nos. 1–3, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakeries and a spice counter inside about eighty metres of each other, with more fish and a butcher's row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the Turkish fishing calendar rather than to a shopping list: commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so palamut lands from September, lüfer through the autumn and hamsi from late autumn into winter, while between mid-April and the end of August almost everything on ice is farmed levrek and çipura or flown in. Fish is chalked per kilo and cleaned at the counter at no charge; produce is priced per kilo too, and the crates behind the stall are usually cheaper than the display. Stall names on this street turn over faster than the trades do, so shop the counter, not the sign — verify any single shop before you make a special trip for it. The tell — Whole palamut in autumn, gutted and scaled at the counter; ripe tomatoes and a bunch of flat parsley from the greengrocer at Güneşlibahçe 9; then the butchers' row for kuzu pirzola. Say "temizlensin" for the fish to be cleaned. Güneşlibahçe Sokağı and Serasker Caddesi, Osmanağa, Kadıköy · Stalls set their own hours; the street trades daytime and is busiest late morning. Verify per shop.

old_cards.group: Two markets, and how to eat standing up in them
old_cards.name: Kadıköy market streets
old_cards.teaser: Chalcedon, the settlement Byzantium's founders were told only the blind would have chosen.
old_cards.body: Megarian Greeks settled here in 685 BC, a generation before Byzantium; the oracle's line about a capital built opposite the city of the blind is a joke at Chalcedon's expense that has outlasted the city. The Turkish name means village of the judge, for Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first kadı after 1453. Today it is a few sloping lanes of fishmongers, picklers and cheese counters, and the correct way through is to eat at every second stall. WHERE Güneşlibahçe Sokak and the lanes around it, Caferağa · ferry from Karaköy or Eminönü

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Salı Pazarı and the weekly pazar circuit
old_cards.teaser: Istanbul's Tuesday market is Kadıköy's, not Beşiktaş's — and it has moved from where its name suggests.
old_cards.body: Worth correcting before you plan a week around it. The Salı Pazarı that Istanbul cooks mean is Kadıköy's, and it no longer stands where the name is remembered: the İSPARK car park on the old ground is still signed Eski Salı Pazarı Otoparkı, while the market itself is mapped up at Hasanpaşa, out towards Kurbağalıdere. Beşiktaş's own weekly street pazar is recorded in OpenStreetMap as a Saturday market, 08:00–20:00, on the ground north-west of Beşiktaş Meydanı, and Bomonti's semt pazarı runs most days with Wednesday off — so the circuit is Tuesday east, Saturday west. The pazar is where price is settled: produce goes for a fraction of shop money, sold by the crate and the kilo, and the last hour before the trestles come down is when growers cut rather than cart it home. The tell — Buy what a shop sells badly and a pazar sells brilliantly: crates of tomatoes for sauce, herbs by the armful, green almonds and unripe plums in spring, quince and pomegranate in autumn. Bring your own bags and small notes — cards are not taken. Salı Pazarı, Hasanpaşa, Kadıköy; Beşiktaş pazarı, north-west of Beşiktaş Meydanı; Bomonti Semt Pazarı, Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6, Şişli · Kadıköy: Tuesday. Beşiktaş: Saturday 08:00–20:00. Bomonti: 09:00–19:30, closed Wednesday (all OpenStreetMap). Confirm the week locally.

p-spice.angle_note: the bazaar and the working street behind it

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar, and what it is now
old_cards.teaser: Eighty-five shops under a 1660 vault, and fewer of them sell spice every year.
old_cards.body: Turhan Hatice Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, commissioned the hall as the revenue arm of the Yeni Cami complex; the court architect Koca Kasım Ağa drew it and it was going up in the last months of 1660, after the Great Fire. There are 85 shops today, and the honest reading is that spice is retreating from them: pre-boxed lokum, pistachio pyramids built for photographs, saffron sold by the gram to people who will never cook with it. One measure of the drift — the Ucuzcular spice house, whose family dates its trade to 1886 and which traded under that name for generations, now runs as Hayfene, sells chiefly online, and states on its own contact page that there is no counter sale at its premises. Treat the hall as architecture and orientation, then walk out of the back gate and buy on Hasırcılar Caddesi. The tell — If you do buy inside, buy only weighable single things you can smell first — Urfa isot, Antep pul biber, dried mint, sumac — and refuse anything pre-boxed with a photograph on the lid. Never accept the first price on saffron. Rüstempaşa Mahallesi, Eminönü, Fatih · Recorded in OpenStreetMap as Mon–Sat 08:00–19:00, Sun 09:30–19:00; individual shops vary.

old_cards.group: Two markets, and how to eat standing up in them
old_cards.name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar
old_cards.teaser: Built to fund a mosque, named after the province that paid for it.
old_cards.body: Commissioned by Hatice Turhan Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, and begun in the last months of 1660 after the great fire of that July. It was the arasta of the New Mosque complex: eighty-five shops whose rent maintained the mosque. The name is Egypt — the building went up on revenues from the Ottoman province, and much of what filled it arrived by the same route. Walk the L, buy nothing, and eat in the streets behind it where the traders do. WHERE Eminönü, beside the New Mosque · the lanes off Hasırcılar Çarşısı are where to eat

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Hasırcılar Caddesi — the working street
old_cards.teaser: The street the bazaar's own traders shop on, running west from the Spice Bazaar's back gate.
old_cards.body: Hasırcılar is where the wholesale rhythm survives: coffee roasters, nut and dried-fruit merchants, cheese, pickle and pulse counters, and a fishmonger — OpenStreetMap maps the roaster Kurukahveci Nuri Toplar and the fish counter Taze Balıkçı directly on it, a hundred metres from the bazaar's tourist trade. Quantities here are assumed in kilos rather than gift boxes, prices are lower than inside the hall for the same goods, and nobody presses a sample on you to start a negotiation. The street works on the same clock as the wholesalers: weekday mornings, while the handcarts are still moving, and many counters are shut on Sunday. This is the buy for bulk pul biber, isot, nar ekşisi, pulses, walnuts and grating cheese. The tell — Ask by weight and in Turkish units — "yarım kilo" for half a kilo, "çeyrek" for a quarter. Taste kaşar before it is cut, and buy pepper flakes here rather than in the hall. Hasırcılar Caddesi, Rüstempaşa, Eminönü, Fatih · Daytime, weekdays busiest; most counters shut by early evening and many close Sunday. Verify per shop.

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Kadınlar Pazarı
old_cards.teaser: The Siirt quarter's larder, trading under the Valens Aqueduct at Zeyrek.
old_cards.body: This is a community market rather than a general one: the streets around it were settled by families from Siirt and the south-east, and the shops carry what that kitchen needs — otlu peynir threaded with wild herbs, thick pistachios, isot, comb honey, dried pulses — alongside the büryan ocakları where lamb hangs in pit ovens cut into the floor. OpenStreetMap records unusually long trading here, roughly 08:00–22:00 Wednesday to Saturday, 08:00–23:00 on Sunday and from 09:00 Monday and Tuesday, which makes it the one provisioning stop on the historic peninsula still working after the bazaar quarters have shuttered for the evening. It sits west of the Spice Bazaar, below the aqueduct arches at Zeyrek — uphill, and worth the walk for the cheese alone. Individual shops keep their own hours inside those bounds. The tell — Buy otlu peynir by the piece and only after tasting: the herb should read as wild garlic and thyme, not as salt carrying a green fleck. Then isot, Siirt pistachios, and a slab of comb honey. Kadınlar Pazarı, Zeyrek, Fatih · Wed–Sat 08:00–22:00; Sun 08:00–23:00; Mon–Tue 09:00–22:00 (OpenStreetMap). Shops vary.

p-besiktas-fish.group: The fish, and the Saturday market

old_cards.group: The markets and the streets behind them
old_cards.name: Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı
old_cards.teaser: The European side's working fish market, wedged into the çarşı two minutes from the ferry.
old_cards.body: Beşiktaş keeps its fish trade in the covered block behind the square, mapped in OpenStreetMap as Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı, and unlike the Beyoğlu row it is still a market before it is a restaurant: whole fish on ice, chalked per kilo, gutted and scaled at the counter for nothing. For anyone provisioning off a Bosphorus berth this is the nearest serious fish counter on the European shore — the argument for it over Kadıköy is simply that you do not cross the water with a cold box. The çarşı around it closes the rest of the list inside a hundred metres: nut and dried-fruit counters, helva makers, a tea seller, greengrocers. Hours are not published for the block, so treat it as a daytime market and go mid-morning. The tell — Learn the lüfer ladder before you buy — çinekop, sarıkanat, lüfer and kofana are one fish at four ages, and Turkey enforces a minimum landing size, so a stall offering you the smallest grade is telling you something about itself. Ask for "temizlensin" and say whether you want it scaled. Beşiktaş çarşı, behind Beşiktaş Meydanı, Beşiktaş · Not published; trades daytime, busiest mid-morning. Verify before a special trip.

p-resat.group: The fish, and the Saturday market

old_cards.group: Counters worth a detour
old_cards.name: Reşat Balık
old_cards.teaser: A fishmonger in the Beyoğlu fish market since 1941 — and one of the few that opens on Sunday.
old_cards.body: The house dates itself to 1941 on its own site and runs two counters: Sahne Sokak No: 8 inside the Balık Pazarı off İstiklal, and Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c at Bostancı on the Asian side. OpenStreetMap records the Beyoğlu shop as Mon–Sat 08:00–20:00 and Sun 08:00–19:00, which matters — most Istanbul fish counters are done by Sunday lunchtime. Be clear-eyed about the setting: the Beyoğlu fish market around it has thinned into meyhane tables and souvenir stalls, so the row is now more restaurant than market and the fish counter is the reason to walk in, not the atmosphere. It is the closest serious fishmonger to Pera and Galata, which is the practical case for it. The tell — Buy to the calendar. Palamut from September, lüfer through the autumn, hamsi from late autumn into winter; Turkish commercial fishing closes 15 April to 1 September, so anything glossy in July is farmed or flown. Have it cleaned at the counter — "temizlensin". Sahne Sokak No: 8, Balık Pazarı, Beyoğlu (also Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c, Bostancı) · Mon–Sat 08:00–20:00, Sun 08:00–19:00 (OpenStreetMap)

p-ferikoy.group: The fish, and the Saturday market

old_cards.group: Counters worth a detour
old_cards.name: Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar
old_cards.teaser: A Saturday producers' market where the residue analyses are on a desk you can walk up to and read.
old_cards.body: The %100 Ekolojik Pazarlar network lists a Şişli market on Saturday, alongside Bakırköy on Friday and Kartal on Sunday, and describes the model in its own words as a "halk pazarı" — a public market where growers sell direct, not a boutique with a certificate on the wall. Certification is backed by field visits and laboratory analyses, and the market keeps a public-relations stall where the inspection reports and residue results for what is on sale can be read on the spot. This is the practical source for the things a city shop handles worst: raw honey, farm eggs, small-dairy cheeses and butter, cold-pressed oils, unsprayed greens. The covered ground is mapped in OpenStreetMap as Bomonti Semt Pazarı at Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6 — the same yard that hosts the Sunday antiques market, so check which day you are walking into. The tell — Ask a stallholder for the analiz raporu; the straight ones point you at the results desk rather than talking about it. Buy honey, eggs, butter and leaves here — not staples, which are cheaper at a semt pazarı. Feriköy covered market ground, Gökkuşağı Sokağı 6, Şişli · Saturday (operator's own listing). Times not published — go in the morning.

old_cards.group: Counters worth a detour
old_cards.name: Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
old_cards.teaser: One counter on Tahmis Sokak that has ground the city's coffee since 1871.
old_cards.body: The house is in its 155th year — its own site runs the anniversary as "155. YIL" and its official channel carries the founding date in the handle — and it is still at Tahmis Sokağı 66, in the purpose-built block the company credits to the architect Zühtü Başar. There are only three shops in the whole city, all confirmed on the company's own contact pages: the Eminönü merkez, a Sirkeci branch, and Kadıköy at Osmanağa Mahallesi, Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 — anything sold as Mehmet Efendi anywhere else is retail packaging, not the counter grind. The queue is long, moves fast, and almost everyone in it buys the same thing: Türk kahvesi ground to order and handed over still warm. The company does not publish shop hours on its own site, which is worth knowing before you cross the Golden Horn for it. The tell — Buy Türk kahvesi ground fresh at the counter, in the smallest pack you will finish within a fortnight — it is milled far finer than espresso and roasted for cezve extraction, so it will choke a portafilter basket. Tahmis Sokağı 66, Eminönü 34116, İstanbul (branch: Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12, Kadıköy 34714) · Not published on the company's own site — confirm before a special trip.

p-namli.angle_note: the deli and what pastırma is

old_cards.group: Counters worth a detour
old_cards.name: Namlı Gurme
old_cards.teaser: One Karaköy counter covering pastırma, cheese, olives, oil, honey and tahin — open seven days a week from seven in the morning.
old_cards.body: This is the single most efficient provisioning stop on the European side, and its own shop publishes the numbers, VAT included: çemeni sıyrılmış pastırma, the fenugreek crust scraped back, ₺5,400/kg; an 850 g kangal sucuk made from 100% beef in the house's own workshop, ₺1,836; Gelibolu eski kaşar ₺1,690/kg and Kars Göle eski kaşar ₺1,080/kg; Erzincan tulum ₺1,180/kg, Van otlu peynir ₺1,490/kg, Ezine beyaz peynir ₺598 a block, Balıkesir buffalo butter ₺576 for 450 g. On the dry side: kuru sele olives ₺780/kg, Ayvalık kırma yeşil ₺590/kg, a litre of Makaron olive oil ₺1,080, 330 g of tahin ₺240, Elazığ mulberry pekmez ₺350 and nar ekşisi ₺350 for 350 ml. Honey is the outlier — Hakkari karakovan comb honey ₺4,200 — and these are the online-store figures checked in August 2026, so the counter can differ. The hours are the real advantage: Monday to Sunday, 07:00 to 22:00. The tell — Pastırma cut to order in front of you, thin enough to read through — ask for the çemeni sıyrılmış if you want the meat rather than the fenugreek. Kangal sucuk whole, not sliced. A kilo of Gelibolu eski kaşar for grating, and tulum for the meze board. Kemankeş Mahallesi, Mumhane Caddesi, Atilla İş Hanı No: 6/A, Karaköy, Beyoğlu · Monday–Sunday 07:00–22:00 (the shop's own listing)

old_cards.group: The counters that outlived the empire
old_cards.name: Pastırma and sucuk
old_cards.teaser: Air-dried beef under a fenugreek crust — and the word pastrami came from.
old_cards.body: Pastırma comes from bastırma, to press. The Ottomans took a Byzantine cured beef called paston and renamed it; Kayseri became the centre, and an 1893 British Foreign Office report already singled the city out for it. The crust is çemen — crushed fenugreek, cumin, garlic and hot paprika — over meat dried hard. Sucuk is its sausage cousin, garlic-heavy, fried for breakfast. English took pastrami by way of Yiddish, perhaps crossed with salami. The cured-meat shops sit along the streets flanking the Spice Bazaar in Eminönü

f-lale.angle_note: pointer, late angle: işkembe against the rakı; the hour it shuts

ref_venue.name: Lale İşkembecisi
ref_venue.address: Tarlabaşı Bulvarı, Taksim/Beyoğlu, İstanbul — the house publishes no street number; use the map link
ref_venue.hours: 24 hours, 7 days — the house's own published claim (site read 2026-08-17)
ref_venue.hook: The 24-hour işkembeci on Tarlabaşı Bulvarı, ladling tripe soup since 1960.
ref_venue.why: The house runs 24 hours, 7 days — its own standing claim, printed across its site — in a restored 300-year-old building, with chef Arif Sarı on the tripe. The menu is freshly repriced in current lira (işkembe ₺300, kuzu paça ₺390) and live ordering runs through Getir Yemek and Trendyol GO, which is how a 1960 institution proves it is still awake.
ref_venue.verdict: The classic ending: the soup that closes a rakı night, in the room that has been closing them for sixty-five years.
ref_venue.caveat: Verified through the house's own live channels — freshly repriced menu, working delivery ordering — rather than recent independent coverage. For a 04:00 crossing of the city, one phone call first.
ref_venue.signature: İşkembe çorbası against the rakı — the Beyoğlu night's traditional last chapter.
ref_venue.person: Founded 1960; the house names Arif Sarı as its chef — 'Lale'nin şefi Arif Sarı işkembeden başka şeyler de yapıyor', its own page says.
ref_venue.price_range: ₺ — işkembe ₺300, kuzu paça ₺390, kuzu kokoreç ₺600 on the current house menu (full-portion prices)
ref_venue.reservation: Walk in, any hour — that is the point. Delivery via Getir Yemek and Trendyol GO.

dishes.name: İşkembe çorbası
dishes.note: the house trade since 1960 — dress it at the table with garlic vinegar and lemon; ₺300 on the current menu

dishes.name: Tuzlama
dishes.note: the richer, larger cut of the tripe — the regulars' bowl; ₺320

dishes.name: Tandır kuzu başı
dishes.note: roast lamb's head from the tandır, for the committed; ₺800

dishes.name: Yaprak ciğer
dishes.note: thin-leaf fried lamb's liver, the plate to share while the soup comes; ₺650

f-kizilkayalar.angle_note: pointer, late angle: the 03:00 wet burger

ref_venue.name: Kızılkayalar
ref_venue.neighborhood: Taksim — Sıraselviler corner of the square
ref_venue.hours: No published hours — the Taksim büfe's reputation is built on the hours nobody else keeps; the after-midnight queue is the institution
ref_venue.hook: The inventor of the islak burger, on the same Taksim corner since 1972.
ref_venue.why: The house history, on its own site: the büfe's foundations were laid on Taksim Meydanı in 1972 — 'Kızılkayalar Hamburger'in temelleri 1972 yılında Taksim Meydanı'nda atılmıştır' — the Kızılkaya family took it over and, six years on, gave it the family name; it was the first büfe in Taksim to serve et döner, and invented the ıslak hamburger — the small garlicky burger soaked in tomato sauce and held sweating in a steam case — after months of recipe trials. The family brands itself 'Islak Hamburgerin Mucidi', and no one seriously disputes it.
ref_venue.verdict: At 03:00 on Sıraselviler this is not a burger, it is the city's agreed way to end a night: a steam-cabinet case glowing at the corner, one bite gone before you have finished paying. Order two immediately; one is a rookie error.
ref_venue.signature: Islak hamburger — the steam-case burger soaked in garlicky tomato sauce
ref_venue.reservation: None. It is a büfe window on the square.

dishes.name: Islak hamburger
dishes.note: the invention itself — sauce-soaked, steam-case warm, gone in four bites

dishes.name: Et döner
dishes.note: the house was the first büfe in Taksim to serve it, per its own history page

dishes.name: Ayran
dishes.note: the only correct drink at that counter at that hour

f-gulluoglu.angle_note: baklava past midnight; the Güllüoğlu split and the PGI told once here

old_cards.group: Baklava and the Güllüoğlu question
old_cards.name: Karaköy Güllüoğlu
old_cards.teaser: One counter in Karaköy, open past midnight, run by the fifth generation of the family that made Gaziantep a baklava town.
old_cards.body: The dynasty's origin is documented outside the family's own marketing: baklava was introduced to Gaziantep in 1871 by Çelebi Güllü, who had learned the recipe from a Syrian chef in Damascus. The city's version was registered as a Turkish geographical indication in 2008 and became Antep Baklavası, a Protected Geographical Indication under the European Commission, in 2013 — the first Turkish product to receive one. This house dates itself to 1843 and puts Nadir Güllü at the counter as "the fifth generation representative of a family that has been making baklava since 1843," trained by his father and master Hacı Mustafa Güllü. The decisive fact is the smallest one: their contact page lists a single shop, Kemankeş Caddesi 67, and OpenStreetMap records the same telephone the house publishes, +90 850 308 45 45, against hours running to one in the morning. The tell — Fıstıklı kuru baklava — the dry pistachio one, no cream, cut small and stacked; it is the version that survives being carried onto a boat. Ask by weight (porsiyon or half a kilo), not by the piece. The tell for the whole city is here: Karaköy Güllüoğlu has one shop, and it is in Karaköy. A Güllüoğlu sign anywhere else is a different branch of the family. Kemankeş Karamustafa Paşa Mah., Kemankeş Cad. No:67, 34425 Karaköy — Beyoğlu · Mon–Sat 07:30–01:00, Sun 08:00–01:00 (OpenStreetMap; the house publishes only a 19:00 courier cut-off)

old_cards.group: Baklava and the Güllüoğlu question
old_cards.name: Faruk Güllü
old_cards.teaser: The counter-lesson: the largest holder of the Güllüoğlu name has quietly stopped putting it on the door.
old_cards.body: Followed by hand on 15 August 2026: gulluoglu.com.tr answers with a 301 to farukgulluoglu.com.tr, which answers with a second 301 to farukgullu.com.tr. The shopfront brand is now "Faruk Güllü Baklava" while the copyright line on that same page still reads "Baklavacı Güllüoğlu Gıda Sanayi ve Dış Ticaret A.Ş." — the company kept the old name, the sign dropped it. The operating address given is a plant on Fırat Plastik Caddesi in Büyükçekmece, an industrial estate at the far western edge of the city, not a shop in the old town. Güllü is a large family and several descendants trade under names built from it; the surname is inherited, the kitchen is not. The tell — Read the first name, not the surname. Nadir Güllü means the single Karaköy shop. Faruk means this operation, which sells through many branches and now leads with the given name. If a Güllüoğlu counter is inside a shopping centre or an airport, it is neither of the two above. That is not a verdict on the pastry — it is a warning against assuming you are eating what you read about. Türkoba Mah., Fırat Plastik Cad. No:35, Büyükçekmece — head office, not a shop

old_cards.group: The counters that outlived the empire
old_cards.name: Baklava
old_cards.teaser: Handed to the Janissaries on the fifteenth of Ramadan; claimed by four cuisines since.
old_cards.body: The one hard Ottoman fact is a ceremony: on the fifteenth of Ramadan the Sultan sent trays of baklava down to the Janissary barracks in a procession called the Baklava Alayı. The origins are genuinely unsettled — Byzantine koptoplakous, Central Asian Turkic layered breads and the Arab lauzinaj of tenth-century cookbooks all have serious advocates. What is settled is the name: since 2013 Gaziantep Baklavası has carried an EU protected geographical indication. Sold citywide · the counters worth the walk are the ones with an oven behind the display

old_cards.group: Lokum, muhallebi, dondurma, boza
old_cards.name: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir
old_cards.teaser: Istanbul's oldest sugar counter, and the one claim about it that the historians will not sign.
old_cards.body: The company's account: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir came to Constantinople from Kastamonu and opened in Bahçekapı in 1777; three generations of the family served as Şekerci Başı, head confectioner to the Ottoman palace; five generations have kept the Bahçekapı shop, which grew from a single room to 88 square metres by swallowing the spice shop next door. Where to be careful is the invention story. The Oxford Companion to Food is blunt — "although Bekir is often credited with the invention, there is no real evidence for it" — and Persian recipes using starch and sugar predate him by centuries. What is not in dispute is that the house still trades: eight points across Istanbul and Ankara, with the İstiklal Caddesi shop recorded open 08:00–21:00 daily and a Kadıköy counter on Muvakkıthane Caddesi. The tell — Ask for lokum cut from the tray rather than a sealed box: sakızlı (mastic) and gül (rose) plain, fıstıklı if you want the pistachio. The second counter is the one people walk past — akide şekeri, the hard palace candy the shop was making before lokum, plus helva and badem ezmesi. The historic address is Bahçekapı, off Hamidiye Caddesi; everything else is a branch. Hamidiye Cad., Hobyar Mah., Bahçekapı-Sirkeci, 34112 Fatih; branches at İstiklal Cad. 83, Beyoğlu and Muvakkıthane Cad. 14-16, Kadıköy · İstiklal Cad. branch Mon–Sun 08:00–21:00 (OpenStreetMap); the house publishes no hours

old_cards.group: The counters that outlived the empire
old_cards.name: Lokum
old_cards.teaser: Starch, sugar and rosewater — and a founding date historians will not sign off.
old_cards.body: The house of Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir dates its Bahçekapı shop to 1777, when its founder came down from Kastamonu; the Oxford Companion to Food notes there is no real evidence for the invention claim, and Tim Richardson has written on how often confectionery dates are commercial rather than historical. The sweet itself is a gel of starch and sugar scented with rosewater, mastic, bergamot or lemon, sometimes loaded with pistachio or walnut. Buy it cut from the tray. WHERE Bahçekapı, Eminönü · a short walk from the Spice Bazaar

old_cards.group: Lokum, muhallebi, dondurma, boza
old_cards.name: Saray Muhallebicisi
old_cards.teaser: A milk-pudding house, not a patisserie — opened in Kasımpaşa in 1935 to feed Beyoğlu properly.
old_cards.body: Founded in 1935 by Hüseyin Topbaş with a stated aim that has survived on the company's own page in the original wording: "Beyoğlu'nda zarif hanımefendi ve beyefendilere tatlıların en güzelini yedirmek" — to feed the elegant ladies and gentlemen of Beyoğlu the finest of desserts. It took fourteen years to make the move that mattered, relocating onto Beyoğlu proper in 1949. The house now counts 21 branches, around 1,400 staff and more than a hundred flavours, and names bal kaymağı, fresh bread, tea and börek among the things it is known for. The İstiklal Caddesi room is the one with the history; the rest are the chain that history paid for. The tell — Order what a muhallebici exists for and what a patisserie cannot make: tavuk göğsü, the pudding thickened with shredded chicken breast until you cannot find it, and kazandibi, the same pudding scorched on the bottom of the pan and served caramelised side up. If it is morning, bal kaymak with bread instead — the house puts it first on its own list. İstiklal Cad., Asmalı Mescit Mah., 34430 Beyoğlu (21 branches in total) · Not published

old_cards.group: Lokum, muhallebi, dondurma, boza
old_cards.name: Vefa Bozacısı
old_cards.teaser: Thick, pale, faintly sour fermented millet, poured at the address that turned it into a trade in September 1876.
old_cards.body: The house's own tarihçe: Hacı Sadık Bey arrived in Istanbul from Prizren in 1870 and spent six winters carrying boza through the streets in copper vessels before opening, in September 1876, what it calls the first registered boza shop in the world. He fixed the style the city still expects and describes it precisely — thick-bodied, pale yellow, caught at the moment the fermentation bubbles first rise, with a very light sourness. His son İsmail Hakkı came into the production; the house says the fourth generation runs it now, and it is the only boza shop of its era still trading. The same firm makes vinegars, üzüm şırası and şerbet, which is what carries it through the months when nobody wants boza. The tell — One glass of boza, standing, taken the customary way — dusted with cinnamon, with roasted leblebi to chew alongside. This is cold-weather drinking: come between October and April and the shop is doing what it exists for; come in August and you are buying vinegar. A glass said to have been used by Atatürk is kept on display. Vefa Cad. No:66, 34134 Fatih — tel +90 212 519 49 22 · OpenStreetMap records Mon–Sun 08:00–22:00; the house publishes no hours of its own

old_cards.group: Baklava and the Güllüoğlu question
old_cards.name: Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası
old_cards.teaser: Künefe cooked the Antakya way, one street off İstiklal, at a house that came north from Hatay.
old_cards.body: Two Istanbul rooms, both verified from the restaurant's own site: İstiklal Caddesi No:39 in Beyoğlu, opposite the French Consulate, and Nispetiye Caddesi No:18 out in Etiler. Künefe is the Hatay dessert and the reason to end a meal here rather than walk on — shredded kadayıf packed around fresh, unsalted, unaged cheese, baked in a shallow copper dish until both faces are dark, then drowned in syrup at the pass. The only credential the house advertises is a TripAdvisor certificate from 2015, which proves nothing at all; judge it on what arrives. OpenStreetMap places the POI just behind the avenue on Meşelik Sokağı, so aim for the İstiklal frontage and expect to turn the corner. The tell — Order the künefe at the end and eat it the moment it lands — it is only itself while the cheese still pulls, and it dies within minutes of the copper. One dish between two after a full Hatay table is enough. Do not order it to take away. İstiklal Cad. No:39 (opposite the French Consulate), Katip Mustafa Çelebi Mah., 34433 Beyoğlu; second room at Nispetiye Cad. No:18 · Not published

old_cards.group: Lokum, muhallebi, dondurma, boza
old_cards.name: Mado
old_cards.teaser: The Kahramanmaraş ice cream you cut with a knife — and the chain that industrialised it, which is both the point and the limit.
old_cards.body: The company's own history page traces the thing back to snow carried down from Ahır Dağı above Kahramanmaraş, which "Osman Ağa" enriched with milk, honey and salep. His descendants Mehmet, Atilla and Erdal Kanbur turned it into an industry — Yaşar Kanbur began by making and selling ice cream from a small shop next to the Aras bus garage — with a Kahramanmaraş factory in 1965, machines in 1970, the MARDO brand in 1984 and real modernisation in 1989. The house dates itself to 1850. Two ingredients do all the work: goat milk, which is why the company runs its own "MADO Beyazı" goat farm, and salep, the ground orchid tuber that makes the ice cream stretch and refuse to melt. Demand for salep has thinned the region's wild orchids badly enough that Turkey banned its export. The tell — Ask for kesme dondurma — the cut ice cream, served in slabs with a knife and fork rather than scooped — and take it sade, plain, so the goat milk and the salep are the flavour. The cone is the tourist version. No single flagship is worth crossing the city for: this is a several-hundred-branch chain and any decent branch will show you what the texture is, which is precisely why it belongs here as a reference point rather than a destination. Branches across the city; no flagship verified

old_cards.group: Lokum, muhallebi, dondurma, boza
old_cards.name: Baylan Pastanesi
old_cards.teaser: The republic's oldest pâtisserie, and one dessert that was invented inside it in 1954.
old_cards.body: Opened in 1923 by Filip Lenas, a Greek of Albanian origin, with his cousin Yorgi Kiriçi — first in Deva Çıkmazı under the name Loryan, the Turkish ear's rendering of "Le Orient" — and moved onto İstiklal Caddesi, into the Luvr Apartmanı, in 1928. The Kadıköy branch that most people now mean by "Baylan" was opened in 1961 by Mikail Lenas. The Kup Griye is the house's own: created by Harry Lenas in 1954, vanilla and caramel ice cream under whipped cream, honeyed almonds and caramel sauce, served with a kedidili biscuit. The business passed to the Altınmarka group, owner of Kahve Dünyası, in 2009 and has kept opening rooms since — Galataport in 2021, Kız Kulesi in 2024 — and its site was live and carrying a 2026 copyright line when checked. The tell — Kup Griye, sitting down, at the Kadıköy shop on Muvakkıthane Caddesi. Ask for it by name; it is the only thing here you cannot get somewhere else, and it is the reason to take a table rather than a paper bag. Note the address carefully — the Hacı Bekir counter is four doors along the same street. Muvakkıthane Cad. No:19, Caferağa Mah., 34710 Kadıköy — tel +90 216 346 63 50 · Not published

old_cards.group: The Turkish-language food press
old_cards.name: Yemek ve Kültür
old_cards.teaser: The scholarly food journal that grew out of a Kadıköy kebab shop.
old_cards.body: First issue January 2005 ; issue 84 is on the table now, four a year, print only, with no overseas subscription offered. Zeynep Dağdeviren is the responsible editor and Musa Dağdeviren sits on the board, filing seven forgotten folk recipes every issue. The advisory board carries Evangelia Balta , the historian of Turkish-speaking Ottoman Orthodox Christians — which tells you how seriously it takes the question of who actually cooked this food. yemekvekultur.com · Instagram @yemekvekulturdergisi_ciya · annual subscription delivers inside Turkey only

old_cards.group: The Turkish-language food press
old_cards.name: Vedat Milor
old_cards.teaser: A Berkeley sociologist who became the country's most argued-with palate.
old_cards.body: Born 1955, schooled at Galatasaray Lisesi, economics at Boğaziçi, a masters at the LSE and a doctorate in sociology at Berkeley whose thesis the American Sociological Association named the best of 1990 . He turned that apparatus on restaurants, first in Milliyet and then in a long-running NTV programme, and edits the English-language Gastromondiale . In Istanbul his verdict moves a booking sheet the way a star does. gastromondiale.com in English · his social feeds and television work are Turkish

old_cards.group: The Turkish-language food press
old_cards.name: Aylin Öney Tan
old_cards.teaser: The one Turkish food writer still filing weekly in English.
old_cards.body: Her column runs in Hürriyet Daily News , Türkiye's oldest English-language daily, and it is current rather than archival — she was filing through July 2026. Recent pieces have covered gastronomic diplomacy at state dinners, the Culture Route Festival mapping fifty taste stops across Bursa, and the seasonal logic Istanbul kitchens actually work to. The best route into Anatolian regional food without a translator. hurriyetdailynews.com, opinion pages · free

v-cb.group: Written in English, reported on the ground

old_cards.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
old_cards.name: Culinary Backstreets
old_cards.teaser: Two men in Istanbul writing up lunch, and they never lost the habit.
old_cards.body: It began as Istanbul Eats , a blog run by Ansel Mullins, who worked in historic restoration, and Yigal Schleifer, then the Christian Science Monitor 's Istanbul correspondent. The site first appears in the web archive in April 2009. It has since grown into food tours and reporting across close to thirty cities, but Istanbul remains the deepest desk, and istanbuleats.com now simply redirects here. culinarybackstreets.com — Istanbul city guide, daily dispatches, walking tours · free to read

v-cornucopia.group: Written in English, reported on the ground

old_cards.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
old_cards.name: Cornucopia
old_cards.teaser: For people who came for the food and stayed for the Ottoman archive.
old_cards.body: Launched in 1992 and made between Scotland, London and Turkey, it now runs two issues a year at a circulation above twenty thousand, edited by John Scott with Berrin Torolsan as publishing director. The register is connoisseurial — architecture, textiles, gardens, Anatolian archaeology — and it treats food as material culture rather than as a booking problem. The complete digital archive of every issue costs about nineteen pounds a year. cornucopia.net · print and digital · digital subscription around GBP 19 a year

v-recap.group: Written in English, reported on the ground

old_cards.group: Written in English, reported on the ground
old_cards.name: Turkey recap
old_cards.teaser: Why the bar you loved is suddenly not serving alcohol.
old_cards.body: Independent and reader-supported, written by journalists based in Ankara and Istanbul; the flagship letter launched in 2019 and now runs politics and foreign affairs on Thursdays, business and economy on Fridays. Diego Cupolo co-founded it with Raziye Akkoç. Not a food publication — but licensing, alcohol regulation, inflation and the lira set what an Istanbul evening costs and whether the meyhane down the road can still pour. turkeyrecap.com · paid with a free trial · Turkish edition at studyorecap.com

v-ohp.group: The history, and what is on the week you land

old_cards.group: The history under the plate
old_cards.name: Ottoman History Podcast
old_cards.teaser: Academics talking properly, without the academic gate.
old_cards.body: Started in March 2011 as an experiment in accessible scholarly production and became one of the largest digital resources of its kind on the Ottoman Empire and the modern Middle East. Chris Gratien, now at the University of Virginia, has recorded more than two hundred interviews. It carries no advertising and takes no revenue, and runs a parallel Turkish-language strand. Search the archive for coffee, wine, famine and the millet system. ottomanhistorypodcast.com · Apple Podcasts and Spotify · full episode guide online

v-iksv.group: The history, and what is on the week you land

old_cards.group: What is actually on, the week you land
old_cards.name: İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts
old_cards.teaser: One foundation programmes most of the big weeks in the Istanbul year.
old_cards.body: It runs the Istanbul Film Festival, the Music Festival, the Jazz Festival, the Theatre Festival, the Istanbul Biennial and the Design Biennial, plus Filmekimi and the year-round Salon İKSV stage, and it curates the Turkish Pavilion at Venice. The calendar and the e-bulletin are the fastest way to learn whether your dates collide with something worth moving a dinner for. Both Turkish and English. iksv.org · calendar and e-bülten sign-up, free

v-timeout.group: The history, and what is on the week you land

old_cards.group: What is actually on, the week you land
old_cards.name: Time Out Istanbul
old_cards.teaser: The English backstop when you need something open tonight.
old_cards.body: Time Out runs a full local Istanbul edition in both English and Türkçe, across restaurants and cafes, things to do, film, music and nightlife, art and culture. It is a commercial listings operation, not a critical guide, and it should never settle an argument about where to eat. For opening hours, one-off events and what has just appeared in the street you are standing in, it is the quickest English source. timeout.com/istanbul · free · English and Turkish editions
